newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HSBC HK bond index rose 0.91 pct to 122.95 in Jan.
newsitem.headline: HSBC HK bond index rose 0.91 pct to 122.95 in Jan.

text.p: HSBC Markets said on Tuesday its Hong Kong bond index rose to 122.95 in January, a 0.91 percent increase over December.
The sub-index for Hong Kong government paper increased by 0.75 percent, while the sub-index for non-Hong Kong government paper rose by 1.03 percent.

Compared with levels at end-January 1996, the overall index increased by 6.1 percent, the sub-index for Hong Kong government paper rose by 5.9 percent and the sub-index for non-Hong Kong government paper increased by 6.2 percent.
U.S. Treasuries drifted lower in early January due to worries that strong economic growth would prompt the U.S. Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy.
A large supply of corporate and government paper was issued, which also weighed on bonds, HSBC said.
Consequently, the 30-year U.S. government bond yield rose 20 basis points during the month to 6.94 percent by January 27.

The subsequent release of softer economic data, however, soothed fears of a possible rate hike at the Fed's policy meeting to be held on February 4-5. This helped the 30-year bond yield to fall to around 6.79 percent by the end of January, HSBC said.
The Hong Kong bond market tends to follow the U.S. Treasury market because Hong Kong's currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar.

The local yield curve steepened in early January, reflecting the market's uncertainty over the near-term rate outlook. The long end later recouped some losses as investor demand increased due to attractive yields.
A good response to the Hong Kong government's second issue of 10-year Exchange Fund notes helped to underpin market sentiment, HSBC said.
HSBC also said that stronger liquidity demand ahead of the Lunar New Year caused the gap between short-dated bond yields and interbank rates to widen significantly towards the end of January.
